::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Condensation grows cloud droplets, but a bigger drop's radius grows more slowly. At 0.5% supersaturation (the air holds 0.5% more water vapor than saturation allows), a 10 µm radius droplet needs about 4.2 days to reach 0.6 mm radius. Once a few drops are large, collection is faster. In an idealized model at 1 g m⁻³, a 20 µm drop reaches 0.6 mm in about 40 min if the collection efficiency $E$ is 1, or about 6.6 h if $E$ is 0.1. Rain becomes likely once the average droplet passes about 13 µm radius.
:::

## The size gap

Here, sizes are radii. A cloud droplet has a radius of about 10 µm. A raindrop has a radius of about 1 mm. The volume of a sphere grows with the cube of its radius, so the volume ratio is

$$\frac{V_\text{rain}}{V_\text{drop}} = \left(\frac{1000\ \mu\text{m}}{10\ \mu\text{m}}\right)^3 = 10^6.$$

The 1 mm value is illustrative, not sourced. Xue and colleagues wrote in 2008 that growth across the 10 to 50 µm radius range had not been fully explained.[^xue2008] This post follows condensation and then collection from 10 µm to 0.6 mm radius, a small raindrop where the fall-speed law used below still applies.

## Condensation narrows the spread of sizes

Condensation makes big drops grow more slowly in radius than small ones. Drops in a cloud therefore become more alike over time. Rogers and Yau give the growth law for a drop in supersaturated air:[^rogers]

$$r\,\frac{dr}{dt} = G\,s$$

Here $r$ is the radius, $t$ is time, and $s$ is the supersaturation as a fraction, so 0.5% means $s = 0.005$. The constant $G \approx 1 \times 10^{-10}$ m² s⁻¹ holds near room temperature. Integrating from a starting radius $r_0$ gives

$$r^2 = r_0^2 + 2Gst.$$

Every drop's $r^2$ grows at the same rate, $2Gs$, so a bigger drop's radius grows more slowly. Its mass still grows faster. The ratio of two radii moves toward one, and a uniform population leaves few larger drops to start collection.

At $s = 0.5\%$, $2Gs = 1 \times 10^{-12}$ m² s⁻¹. Two growth times follow:

- 10 µm to 20 µm: $t = (4 - 1) \times 10^{-10} / 10^{-12} = 300$ s, or 5.0 min.
- 10 µm to 0.6 mm: $t \approx 3.6 \times 10^{-7} / 10^{-12} = 3.6 \times 10^{5}$ s, or 4.2 days.

Growing the drop 60-fold in radius takes 4.2 days, about 300 times the 20 min that Sardina and colleagues name as comparable to the time of rain formation.[^sardina2015] Turbulence can keep the spread wide. In their simulation, condensation in turbulent clouds kept broadening the droplet size distribution.[^sardina2015]

## Collection takes over

A drop that falls faster runs into smaller drops and collects them. [How drops merge](drop-coalescence.qmd) covers what happens at a single contact. Here a collector of radius $R$ falls at speed $v(R)$ through cloud droplets of radius $r_c = 10$ µm, which fall at $v(r_c)$. The collector grows at

$$\frac{dR}{dt} = \frac{E\,L\,[v(R) - v(r_c)]}{4\rho_w}$$

where $L$ is the liquid water content (the mass of cloud water per volume of air, in kg m⁻³), $E$ is the collection efficiency, and $\rho_w = 1000$ kg m⁻³ is the density of water. One g m⁻³ equals $10^{-3}$ kg m⁻³. Only the speed difference matters, since a drop cannot catch droplets falling at its own speed. The formula assumes 10 µm droplets, no updrafts, and constant water content.

The fall speed depends on size in two ranges, according to Rogers and Yau.[^rogers] Below 40 µm, drag follows Stokes law, the drag law for small drops, and

$$v = k_1 R^2, \qquad k_1 = 1.19 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-1}.$$

From 40 µm to 0.6 mm, the speed is linear in radius:

$$v = k_3 R, \qquad k_3 = 8 \times 10^{3}\ \text{s}^{-1}.$$

A 10 µm droplet falls at 1.2 cm/s. At 40 µm, the two fits give 0.19 m/s and 0.32 m/s. They do not meet, so the speed jumps at 40 µm. This post keeps the jump instead of smoothing it.

Collection speeds up as a drop grows, the reverse of condensation. Starting at 20 µm radius with $L = 1$ g m⁻³ and $E = 1$, the drop needs 16 min to reach 40 µm and 23 min more to reach 0.6 mm. The total is 39 min. Time scales as $1/(EL)$, so halving $E$ doubles the time.

| Liquid water content $L$ | Time with $E = 1$ | Time with $E = 0.5$ |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 g m⁻³ | 79 min | 157 min |
| 1 g m⁻³ | 39 min | 79 min |
| 2 g m⁻³ | 20 min | 39 min |

**Table 1.** Idealized time from 20 µm to 0.6 mm radius by collection, from the closed forms in the callout below.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: the collection law and its closed forms

A collector of radius $R$ sweeps out an area $\pi R^2$ each second, at the relative speed $v(R) - v(r_c)$. It catches the fraction $E$ of the water in that volume, so it gains mass at the rate $\pi R^2 E L [v(R) - v(r_c)]$. A drop's mass is $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho_w$, so $4\pi R^2 \rho_w\,dR/dt = \pi R^2 E L [v(R) - v(r_c)]$. Dividing both sides by $4\pi R^2 \rho_w$ gives the law above. The factor $R^2$ cancels.

Below 40 µm, $v(R) - v(r_c) = k_1 (R^2 - r_c^2)$. With $a = E L k_1 / (4\rho_w)$, the time from $R_0$ to $R_1$ is

$$t = \frac{1}{2 a r_c}\left[\ln\frac{R - r_c}{R + r_c}\right]_{R_0}^{R_1}.$$

Above 40 µm, $v(R) - v(r_c) = k_3 (R - R_*)$, where $R_* = v(r_c)/k_3 = 1.5$ µm. With $b = E L k_3 / (4\rho_w)$,

$$t = \frac{1}{b}\ln\frac{R_1 - R_*}{R_0 - R_*}.$$

The 20 to 40 µm step uses the first form and the 40 µm to 0.6 mm step uses the second. A drop of exactly 10 µm radius has zero growth rate in this model, because $R^2 - r_c^2 = 0$.
:::

Starting at 13 µm takes about 66 min at $L = 1$ g m⁻³ and $E = 1$, which is 27 min longer than starting at 20 µm.

Beard and Ochs wrote that collection efficiencies for the droplet sizes that start coalescence were poorly known in 1993, and that they needed laboratory work.[^beard1993] So $E$ is a setting in this post, not a measured value. The growth rate is close to zero near 10 µm, so collection barely starts until some drops are bigger. That is why the head start matters.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
fig1 = {
  // Idealized toy model. Radii in µm, times in minutes.
  const G = 1e-10, s = 0.005, rho = 1000, k1 = 1.19e8, k3 = 8e3;
  const rc = 10e-6, Rstar = k1 * rc * rc / k3;
  const L = 1e-3, E = 1;   // 1 g m⁻³ in kg m⁻³
  const a = E * L * k1 / (4 * rho), b = E * L * k3 / (4 * rho);
  const logspace = (lo, hi, n) => Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => 10 ** (Math.log10(lo) + i * (Math.log10(hi) - Math.log10(lo)) / (n - 1)));

  // Condensation from 10 µm: t = (r^2 - r0^2) / (2 G s), in minutes.
  const cond = logspace(10, 600, 300).map(r => ({r, t: ((r * 1e-6) ** 2 - rc ** 2) / (2 * G * s) / 60}));
  const rCondAt = t => Math.sqrt(rc * rc + 2 * G * s * t * 60) * 1e6;

  // Collection from 20 µm: closed forms from the callout, in minutes.
  const tOf = Rum => {
    const R = Rum * 1e-6;
    const R1 = Math.min(R, 40e-6);
    const part1 = (1 / a) / (2 * rc) * (Math.log((R1 - rc) / (R1 + rc)) - Math.log((20e-6 - rc) / (20e-6 + rc)));
    const part2 = R > 40e-6 ? (1 / b) * Math.log((R - Rstar) / (40e-6 - Rstar)) : 0;
    return (part1 + part2) / 60;
  };
  const coll = logspace(20, 600, 300).map(r => ({r, t: tOf(r)}));

  const timeTick = d => d < 60 ? `${d} min` : d < 1440 ? `${d / 60} h` : `${d / 1440} day${d >= 2880 ? "s" : ""}`;

  return Plot.plot({
    width: Math.min(width, 720),
    height: 380,
    marginLeft: 70,
    style: {background: "transparent", color: "currentColor"},
    x: {type: "log", label: "Time (log scale) →", domain: [1, 6500], ticks: [1, 10, 60, 360, 1440, 4320], tickFormat: timeTick, grid: true},
    y: {type: "log", label: "↑ Drop radius", domain: [10, 600], ticks: [10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 600], tickFormat: d => d + " µm", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(cond, {x: "t", y: "r", stroke: "#f59e0b", strokeWidth: 2.5, strokeDasharray: "7 4"}),
      Plot.line(coll, {x: "t", y: "r", stroke: "#38bdf8", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.text([{t: 2500, r: rCondAt(2500), txt: "Condensation only (dashed)"}],
        {x: "t", y: "r", text: "txt", textAnchor: "end", dy: -10, fill: "currentColor"}),
      Plot.text([{t: 39, r: 600, txt: "Collection from 20 µm (solid)"}],
        {x: "t", y: "r", text: "txt", textAnchor: "end", dx: -8, dy: 4, fill: "currentColor"})
    ]
  });
}
```

**Figure 1.** Idealized toy model (illustrative) of drop radius against time, both on log scales. The dashed orange curve is condensation from 10 µm at $s = 0.5\%$, with $G = 1 \times 10^{-10}$ m² s⁻¹; it needs about 5 min to reach 20 µm. The solid blue curve is collection from 20 µm with $L = 1$ g m⁻³ and $E = 1$, using 10 µm collected droplets. Its speed jumps at 40 µm, where the fall-speed law changes. The model ignores updrafts.

::: {.sim-card}
#### How long to make a raindrop?

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof Lw = Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Liquid water content L (g m⁻³)"})
viewof Ew = Inputs.range([0.01, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.01, label: "Collection efficiency E"})

// Idealized closed forms from the callout. Radii in µm; result in minutes from 20 µm.
tColl = {
  const L = Lw * 1e-3, E = Ew;
  const rho = 1000, k1 = 1.19e8, k3 = 8e3, rc = 10e-6;
  const a = E * L * k1 / (4 * rho), b = E * L * k3 / (4 * rho);
  const Rstar = k1 * rc * rc / k3;
  return Rum => {
    const R = Rum * 1e-6;
    const R1 = Math.min(R, 40e-6);
    const part1 = (1 / a) / (2 * rc) * (Math.log((R1 - rc) / (R1 + rc)) - Math.log((20e-6 - rc) / (20e-6 + rc)));
    const part2 = R > 40e-6 ? (1 / b) * Math.log((R - Rstar) / (40e-6 - Rstar)) : 0;
    return (part1 + part2) / 60;
  };
}
collMin = tColl(600)
condDays = ((600e-6) ** 2 - (10e-6) ** 2) / (2 * 1e-10 * 0.005) / 86400
fmtMin = m => m < 120 ? `${m.toFixed(0)} min` : m < 2880 ? `${(m / 60).toFixed(1)} h` : `${(m / 1440).toFixed(1)} days`
curveW = Array.from({length: 201}, (_, i) => {
  const R = 20 * 30 ** (i / 200);
  return {t: tColl(R), R};
})
html`<div class="sim-readouts">
  <div class="sim-readout"><div class="sim-readout-label">Collection, 20 µm to 0.6 mm</div><div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:#38bdf8">${fmtMin(collMin)}</div></div>
  <div class="sim-readout"><div class="sim-readout-label">Condensation, 10 µm to 0.6 mm, s = 0.5%</div><div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:#f59e0b">${condDays.toFixed(1)} days</div></div>
</div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 300,
  marginLeft: 60,
  style: {background: "transparent", color: "#cbd5e1"},
  x: {label: "Time from 20 µm (min) →", domain: [0, collMin * 1.05], grid: true},
  y: {label: "↑ Drop radius (µm)", domain: [0, 640], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([40], {stroke: "#cbd5e1", strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "2 3"}),
    Plot.line(curveW, {x: "t", y: "R", stroke: "#38bdf8", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.text([{t: 0, R: 40, txt: "40 µm: fall-speed law changes"}],
      {x: "t", y: "R", text: "txt", textAnchor: "start", dy: -8, fill: "#cbd5e1"}),
    Plot.text([{t: collMin, R: 600, txt: "Collection (solid)"}],
      {x: "t", y: "R", text: "txt", textAnchor: "end", dy: -10, fill: "#38bdf8"})
  ]
})
```

**Figure 2.** Idealized collection from 20 µm radius for the $L$ and $E$ you choose. Collected droplets have 10 µm radius, there are no updrafts, and $L$ is constant. Stokes law applies below 40 µm and the linear law above, so the speed jumps at 40 µm. Times scale as $1/(EL)$. The condensation readout is fixed at $s = 0.5\%$.
:::

## Where the head start comes from

Collection needs some larger drops to start. [Köhler theory](kohler-theory.qmd) covers which particles become droplets at all.

Freud and Rosenfeld found that rain becomes likely once the mean volume radius, the average droplet radius weighted by volume, passes about 13 µm. An effective radius, an average that weights bigger drops more heavily, of about 14 µm gives the same threshold.[^freud2012] Their coalescence rate scales as about the fifth power of that radius, so doubling it multiplies the rate by about 32.[^freud2012]

Pollution delays the head start. In deep convective clouds in Israel and India, the cloud depth needed for rain rose by about 280 m for every 100 cm⁻³ more droplets at cloud base.[^freud2012] Very polluted clouds must grow well above the freezing level before rain forms.

Thicker, cleaner stratocumulus, a low and flat cloud layer, drizzles more readily.[^wood2012]^,^[^vanzanten2005] Albrecht proposed that more aerosol reduces drizzle and so can increase low cloud amount. That was a hypothesis, not a measured result.[^albrecht1989]

In a model of small cumulus clouds, turbulence shortened the time to form drizzle by about 40%.[^xue2008] Giant particles may also trigger rain, but in 1993 Beard and Ochs still asked under what conditions they do.[^beard1993]

## What this means for you

Warm rain is a large share of tropical rain, but the share depends on the definition. Lau and Wu used data from the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM), a satellite. They defined warm rain by the radar echo top and found that it gave 31% of tropical rain amount and 72% of tropical rain area.[^lau2003] Liu and Zipser counted rain from clouds whose tops are warmer than 0 °C. Those pixels gave 20% of rainfall over tropical oceans and 7.5% over tropical land.[^liu2009] About half of the ocean pixels and two-thirds of the land pixels sit at the edges of cold systems that contain ice, so the share formed without ice is smaller than those figures.

## Key takeaways

- Sizes here are radii. A 1 mm radius raindrop holds about a million times the water of a 10 µm droplet.
- Condensation alone is slow. At 0.5% supersaturation, a 10 µm drop needs about 4.2 days to reach 0.6 mm radius.
- Collection speeds up as drops grow, but only once a few are large. In the idealized model at 1 g m⁻³, 20 µm to 0.6 mm takes about 39 min with $E = 1$ and about 6.6 h with $E = 0.1$. Starting from 13 µm with $E = 1$ takes about 66 min.
- Rain becomes likely once the mean volume radius passes about 13 µm. Each extra 100 cm⁻³ of droplets needs about 280 m more cloud depth before rain forms.
- Warm rain gives 31% of tropical rain amount under Lau and Wu's echo-top definition. Warm-topped clouds give 20% over tropical oceans and 7.5% over land under Liu and Zipser's cloud-top definition. The number depends on the definition.

[^xue2008]: Xue, Y., Wang, L.-P. & Grabowski, W. W. Growth of cloud droplets by turbulent collision-coalescence. *J. Atmos. Sci.* **65**, 331-356 (2008). https://doi.org/10.1175/2007JAS2406.1
[^rogers]: Rogers, R. R. & Yau, M. K. *A Short Course in Cloud Physics*. 3rd ed. Pergamon Press (1989).
[^sardina2015]: Sardina, G., Picano, F., Brandt, L. & Caballero, R. Continuous growth of droplet size variance due to condensation in turbulent clouds. *Phys. Rev. Lett.* **115**, 184501 (2015). https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.184501
[^beard1993]: Beard, K. V. & Ochs, H. T. Warm-rain initiation: an overview of microphysical mechanisms. *J. Appl. Meteorol.* **32**, 608-625 (1993). https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0450(1993)032<0608:WRIAOO>2.0.CO;2
[^freud2012]: Freud, E. & Rosenfeld, D. Linear relation between convective cloud drop number concentration and depth for rain initiation. *J. Geophys. Res. Atmos.* **117**(D2), 2011JD016457 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1029/2011JD016457
[^albrecht1989]: Albrecht, B. A. Aerosols, cloud microphysics, and fractional cloudiness. *Science* **245**, 1227-1230 (1989). https://doi.org/10.1126/science.245.4923.1227
[^vanzanten2005]: vanZanten, M. C., Stevens, B., Vali, G. & Lenschow, D. H. Observations of drizzle in nocturnal marine stratocumulus. *J. Atmos. Sci.* **62**, 88-106 (2005). https://doi.org/10.1175/JAS-3355.1
[^wood2012]: Wood, R. Stratocumulus clouds. *Mon. Weather Rev.* **140**, 2373-2423 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1175/MWR-D-11-00121.1
[^lau2003]: Lau, K. M. & Wu, H. T. Warm rain processes over tropical oceans and climate implications. *Geophys. Res. Lett.* **30**(24), 2003GL018567 (2003). https://doi.org/10.1029/2003GL018567
[^liu2009]: Liu, C. & Zipser, E. J. "Warm rain" in the tropics: seasonal and regional distributions based on 9 yr of TRMM data. *J. Clim.* **22**, 767-779 (2009). https://doi.org/10.1175/2008JCLI2641.1
